title: Negative binomial regression
biology: Parasite abundance and fish body length
design: Independent fish vary in body length; parasite burdens are highly variable.
data_characteristics: Conditional variance can exceed the conditional mean
other_examples: Microbial colony counts with heterogeneous rates
question: Does expected parasite burden change with fish length?
null: The length coefficient is zero: expected parasite abundance does not change with length in this model.
options: Exponentiate a scaled coefficient to report a meaningful rate ratio.
assumptions: The log mean is modeled appropriately.
A negative binomial mean–variance pattern is plausible.
parametric: Compare residual patterns with Poisson and quasi-Poisson alternatives.
Use a mixed negative binomial model for fish clustered by site.
nonparametric: Bootstrap independent fish or sites for uncertainty.
A rank-based association test asks a different question from a count-model slope.

plot_args.note: Show the conditional mean, not an individual prediction.
Include length units in the axis.

code_simulate:
set.seed(3112)
d <- data.frame(fish = 1:130, length_cm = runif(130, 18, 42))
mu <- exp(-.2 + .085 * d$length_cm)
d$parasites <- rnbinom(130, mu = mu, size = 2)
write.csv(d, file.path(out_dir, "data.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
code_plot:
p <- ggplot2::ggplot(d, ggplot2::aes(length_cm, parasites)) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(alpha = .55, size = 2, color = "#555555") +
  ggplot2::geom_line(data = grid, ggplot2::aes(y = mean_count),
                    color = "#126887", linewidth = 1.3) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "Fish length (cm)", y = "Parasite count") +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 17)
print(p)
code_analysis:
fit <- MASS::glm.nb(parasites ~ length_cm, data = d)
b <- coef(fit)["length_cm"]
se <- sqrt(vcov(fit)["length_cm", "length_cm"])
p_value <- summary(fit)$coefficients["length_cm", "Pr(>|z|)"]
rate_ratio <- exp(5 * b)
ci <- exp(5 * (b + c(-1, 1) * 1.96 * se))
practice: If variance still increases faster than the fitted model predicts, what should you inspect before interpreting its p-value?
generating_model: Generate 130 independent fish with length Uniform(18,42) cm. Parasite count follows a negative binomial with mean exp(-0.2 + 0.085 × length) and size/theta 2. Conditional variance is mean + mean²/2.
generating_truth: The length coefficient is 0.085, so 5 cm multiplies expected parasite abundance by exp(0.425) ≈ 1.530. The slope-zero null is false; the Poisson variance assumption is intentionally violated.
teaching_point: Overdispersion can be addressed with a parametric count model; it does not automatically require replacing the scientific question with a rank test.
